title: Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam bail pleas go to three-judge bench; no interim relief yet
dek: The Chief Justice's bench declined to consider interim bail for now and sent the pleas to a larger bench, citing a conflict between rulings on long custody under the UAPA.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday issued notice to the Delhi Police on fresh bail pleas by activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in the 2020 Delhi riots "larger conspiracy" case, but declined to consider their requests for interim bail until it had heard the police. It also asked for the cases to be placed before the Chief Justice so that a three-judge bench can be formed to hear them.

The bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said the interim bail requests would be taken up only after the Delhi Police responded. "You have made a prayer for interim relief; let it be responded," Justice Bagchi said, according to reports of the hearing. When senior advocate Kapil Sibal, for Mr Khalid, pressed for interim relief, the Chief Justice replied: "Not today."

## Why a larger bench

The referral follows a conflict between two lines of Supreme Court rulings on bail under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), which sets strict conditions for releasing an accused before trial.

In 2021, a three-judge bench in the case of K.A. Najeeb held that long incarceration and delays in trial can justify bail despite those conditions. On 5 January this year, a two-judge bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and N.V. Anjaria denied bail to Mr Khalid and Mr Imam, describing them as "ideological drivers" of the alleged conspiracy, while granting bail to five co-accused, including Gulfisha Fatima, on the ground that their roles were different. Another two-judge bench later criticised that judgment for diluting the Najeeb ruling, and on 22 May Justice Kumar's bench referred the apparent conflict to a larger bench in a case involving a co-accused, Tasleem Ahmed, according to reports.

The Chief Justice remarked that the Najeeb judgment under discussion was his own. "It was my judgment which is being discussed. So I am feeling little embarrassed," he said, according to reports.

## What each side argued

Mr Sibal said Mr Khalid had been in custody for more than six years and pointed out that the bench that made the May reference had granted interim bail to Tasleem Ahmed at the same time. Senior advocate Siddharth Dave, for Mr Imam, argued that the reference had no bearing on these petitions, which were filed under the January judgment's own terms.

That judgment allowed the two men to apply again for bail after the protected witnesses had been examined or after one year, whichever came first. Their lawyers say the prosecution has not yet examined those witnesses and that the one-year period has almost run out. The trial court and the Delhi High Court rejected their renewed applications earlier this year; reports differ on the date of the High Court's decision.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, for the Delhi Police, told the court that the May reference had been made in the same FIR.

## Background

The case concerns the communal violence in north-east Delhi in February 2020, in which 53 people were killed. The Delhi Police allege that the violence was the result of a pre-planned conspiracy and have charged Mr Khalid, Mr Imam and others under the UAPA. The accused deny the charges and say they took part only in peaceful protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act. The trial has not yet concluded.

## What happens next

The Chief Justice said the main bail petitions, not just the interim requests, would be listed before the three-judge bench, after Mr Sibal asked for an early hearing. No date has been reported. The bench's eventual ruling on how the Najeeb principle applies is likely to affect bail in other long-running UAPA cases, not only this one.
